title: Peeling, the solver and families
goal: How the generator picks one primary outline per word across the whole vocabulary: peeling, the exact matching solver, the cost of leaving a word unplaced, and how word families follow their root's stroke.

blocks.x: Peeling: commit the uncontested words first

Every word has a cost-ordered candidate list (see [candidates and cost](#/ref/how-candidates-cost)). Two words may not share an outline, so choices are settled together. Peeling settles the uncontested majority before the solver runs.

items: A word's cheapest remaining candidate is **committed** when its text appears in no other remaining word's list at all.
Committing it removes that text from every other word's list.
That can leave another word with a candidate that is now uniquely its own. Repeat until no word's cheapest text is uniquely its own (a fixed point).

blocks.x: Taking a text nobody else wants never worsens the total, so peeling is exact: no word loses an outline the solver would have given it.

pass : { PAS }            -> committed  pass -> PAS
                           PAS removed from every other list
past : { PAS, PAFT }  -> { PAFT }  -> committed in round 2  past -> PAFT

Words with no candidate skip peeling and the solver and are reported unplaced. In the current build 18,973 of the 100,000 commonest words are still contested after peeling and go to the solver (gold-only words settled beside them, [see below](#/ref/how-candidates-cost), not counted).
The solver: exact min-cost matching

The contested remainder is an assignment problem: words on one side, candidate texts on the other, each text usable by at most one word. The solver finds the cheapest assignment **in total**, not word by word. Hand-written (successive shortest augmenting paths), run per connected component of the contested graph, no graph library.

head: Part
What it is
rows: source, then each word (capacity 1), then each candidate text (capacity 1, cost = that candidate's edge cost), then sink
the candidate's cost (strokes, keys, ergonomics) times the word's frequency weight, so a common word's extra key outweighs a rare word's
one private edge from every word to the sink, used only when a cluster has more words than texts; cost below

Dijkstra with Johnson potentials, started from zero (all costs non-negative); each search stops at the sink and every potential is capped at the sink's distance, keeping reduced costs non-negative; each edge stores its reverse edge's index inline
solved independently, on every core; the largest has about 3,700 words and takes about 1.3 s
300 random over-subscribed graphs, escapes included, are compared with brute force on every test run

blocks.x: Worked example: one, won, wan
Three words compete for the same phonetic texts. The cheapest total matching gives each a different one; a word-by-word greedy pass would give the best text to whichever word came first.

Outline
Why

blocks.x: What it costs to leave a word unplaced
A word with no outline is fingerspelled, so the escape edge charges that cost, always at least one stroke worse than the word's own worst candidate.

no_match_cost(word) = weight * max( letters(word) * STROKE_WEIGHT,
                                    worst_candidate_cost + STROKE_WEIGHT )
STROKE_WEIGHT = 25,000   (one stroke = 25 keys; one key = 1,000)

A crowded cluster such as `ERL` (early, errol, earle, earl) has more members than the four-rung star ladder has texts, so someone is left out. Leaving a rare name unplaced costs less than an extra stroke on a common word, so the common word keeps its one stroke. Words that got a one-stroke outline this way:
In the current build 371 words are unplaced, all rarer than rank 20,000, each still reachable by fingerspelling or a backup entry (see [backups](#/ref/how-backups-output)).

A common word's non-phonetic candidate can take a rarer word's only derivable stroke (Plover's misstroke `TARBG` for dark, repaired to `ARBG`, is also the plain reading of arc and ark). No surcharge. The displaced word goes to the star ladder, then its stem-plus-suffix reading, then `/+*`. See [collisions](#/ref/collisions).
Word families

A family shares its root's stroke (otherwise build was Plover's `PWHR` while builds was the unrelated `PWEULDZ`). `src/family.rs` links words into families; settling runs twice so members can follow their root.
Who is family

rows: `-s -ed -ing -er -est -ly -ness -ment -able -ful -less -ship -hood`, matched by spelling (e-drop, consonant undoubling, i to y, -es/-ies) and confirmed by the sounds the ending adds. Most frequent valid stem wins: robber is rob + -er, not the name robb
`re- pre- un- dis- mis- over- under-` in front of another word whose pronunciation the word ends with
about 150 past tenses and participles and 7 plurals listed in `rules/families.toml` (built from build, men from man)
coincidences that pass every check (better is not bet + -er, moment is not mo + -ment), also listed in `rules/families.toml`

blocks.x: A join through an ending needs a stem of three letters or more; a word in `-ly` never joins through `-y`.
The family rules

After the first settling pass every family root is locked to the outline it won on cost alone: nothing else may take it, and it moves only to something strictly cheaper. Every member is then offered its root's outline, written by these rules, on the root's **last stroke**:

head: Rule
Example
rows: Key already there: add the star
Prefix: its stroke, then the stem

blocks.x: A family offer counts two keys cheaper than it is ([the two-key family preference](#/ref/syllables/the-two-key-family-preference)); it never buys a stroke. A one-stroke brief that beats the family shape by more than two keys is kept (guys stays [[guys|AOEUS]]).
The final pass: lock the top 5,000, then every skeleton

items: A word ranked past 8,000 holds its one-stroke consonant skeleton out of the family passes.
Settling repeats until the offers stop changing, or for at most four passes.
The 5,000 commonest words are locked to what they settled on: nobody else may take those texts, and no locked word may take another's.
One last pass runs with every skeleton in.

A word said at most 200 times that holds a stroke kept as an extra by a word at least 30 times as common gives it up (see [collisions](#/ref/collisions)): it moves to its cheapest free candidate that is not kept either, or has no primary.
Any word on a worse outline than one of its own candidates that nobody holds (a text a root reserved and then left) moves to it, but never to a stroke it just gave up.
Everything is then settled again from scratch.
